findings.issue_text: [BUG] The new `return nil, err` in Authenticate returns TagDevice's plain `error` value as the method's second return, but the hunk's own header shows Authenticate returns an authn-qualified type pair `(*authn.Identity, *authn.Error)` per the repo's authn Client contract, so the package does not type-check. go build fails with `cannot use err (variable of type error) as *authn.Error value in return statement`, breaking compilation of pkg/services/anonymous and every package that imports it — the entire grafana backend binary and all CI jobs on this PR fail before any behavior is testable.

[BUG] The diff adds `var ErrDeviceLimitReached = fmt.Errorf("device limit reached")` without adding the `fmt` import it requires: no hunk touches this file's import block (it ends at line 13, before the first hunk), and the pre-change file cannot already import `fmt` because Go rejects unused imports and no pre-existing function in the file uses it — the hunk line math (`@@ -13,10 +13,14 @@` and every later hunk offset of exactly +4) confirms zero lines are inserted before line 13. Applying this diff leaves database.go with `undefined: fmt`, failing the build of pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/anonstore and everything downstream (the grafana server binary, vet, and all tests), so the feature cannot compile or ship.

[ADVISORY] TagDevice moved from a fire-and-forget goroutine (2-minute `context.WithTimeout`, a `recover()` around panics, and a detached `context.Background()`) onto the synchronous authentication path using the raw request context, which carries no deadline. Operators of anonymous-enabled (public-dashboard) Grafana deployments get every cache-expired (~29 minutes per device) anonymous request blocking on DB I/O with no cap: a slow or hung database now stalls anonymous auth indefinitely where it previously cost one background warning after at most 2 minutes, and any panic inside TagDevice — which the deleted `recover()` existed to swallow — now 500s the request instead of logging a warning.

[ADVISORY] When `device_limit > 0`, CreateOrUpdateDevice issues an extra windowed CountDevices query on every invocation before choosing upsert vs update, with no batch or caching layer in between. Every anonymous request whose device_id misses the 29-minute local cache pays a second DB round-trip, and the count is a range scan over anon_device whose cost grows with table size (this diff adds no index for the counted window; device_id is the only key), so the high-volume anonymous fleets this limit targets add a scan per uncached request exactly during the traffic spikes the limit exists to contain.

[ADVISORY] The 30-day device horizon is now duplicated as two independently hand-maintained constants in different packages: `anonymousDeviceExpiration` in api.go (line 18) and `anonymousDeviceExpiration` in anonstore/database.go (line 16), kept in sync only by naming convention. The admin device-list window (GET /api/devices, built from api.go's copy) and the limit-count/update window (built from the store's copy) must move together; a future edit to one silently desyncs them, leaving operators debugging device-limit rejections against a device list whose window no longer matches what the limit counts.

[BUG] CreateOrUpdateDevice enforces the device limit with a non-atomic count-then-insert sequence: CountDevices and the subsequent upsert run in separate sessions with no lock, transaction, or constraint tying them together. Concurrent first requests from distinct devices (multi-instance Grafana behind one database, or a deliberate parallel request burst — exactly the anonymous traffic the limit targets) each read count < deviceLimit and each insert, so the configured device limit is exceeded and the cap the feature exists to enforce is bypassable.

[BUG] Authenticate now runs TagDevice synchronously on the request path while deleting both the panic-recovery defer and the 2-minute timeout that previously isolated tagging from authentication. A slow or hung database now blocks every cache-miss anonymous request for as long as the client holds the connection (previously tagging was abandoned after 2 minutes off-path and never delayed or failed a response), and a panic inside TagDevice — the exact case the removed recover() existed to contain — now propagates into the auth flow and fails the request instead of being logged as a warning.

[ADVISORY] The only new limit test (TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit) asserts rejection of an unknown device; no test in the diff covers the acceptance criterion that a known, in-window device is still successfully updated through updateDevice when count >= deviceLimit. A regression in updateDevice's WHERE window silently locks out every returning anonymous device the moment the limit is reached, and the suite stays green because the update-success path — the path all legitimate returning users depend on — is never exercised.

[ADVISORY] The new errors.Is(err, anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached) -> return nil, err branch has zero test coverage in the diff, and the PR pins no acceptance criterion for the HTTP response an over-limit anonymous user receives when this raw store error propagates through authn. The rejection UX is left to whatever the generic authn error handler does with a non-sentinel error, so an over-limit visitor gets an arbitrary failure (raw "device limit reached" rendered as an internal error, with error-level log noise per blocked request) and any change to the error type or its rendering ships with no failing test.

[BUG] updateDevice interprets rowsAffected == 0 exclusively as "device limit reached", but on MySQL (go-sql-driver default changed-rows semantics, no CLIENT_FOUND_ROWS in Grafana's DSN) a matched row whose written values are identical also yields 0 affected rows. When two Grafana instances behind a load balancer re-tag the same known device within the same wall-clock second (the per-instance localCache does not deduplicate across pods, and updated_at columns are second-precision), the second instance's value-identical UPDATE reports 0 changed rows, ErrDeviceLimitReached is returned, and the returning user's anonymous request is wrongly rejected.

[ADVISORY] ProvideAnonymousDeviceService dropped its injected anonstore.AnonStore parameter and now constructs the concrete AnonDBStore itself via anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore(sqlStore, cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit), orphaning the previously-consumed DI-provided store binding. Test fakes and any alternate AnonStore implementation can no longer be wired into the service — the diff's own impl_test.go now has to reach into the private anonService.anonStore field to list devices (impl_test.go:124) — so the injectability seam the AnonStore interface exists for is silently gone and the next store-level test or store override requires another constructor refactor.

[ADVISORY] The new [auth.anonymous] device_limit key is read here but the diff ships no corresponding conf/defaults.ini entry or documentation update, breaking Grafana's convention that every configurable setting appears in the shipped template. Operators who configure anonymous access from the shipped defaults.ini or the documented settings reference never learn the option exists, so the "configurable device limit" this PR adds is undiscoverable in practice and the feature goes unused in deployments that would want it.

[ADVISORY] anonymousDeviceLimit is added to the frontend config contract as number | undefined with no consumer anywhere in the diff, while FrontendSettingsDTO (pkg/api/dtos/frontend_settings.go:195, no omitempty) always serializes the field — including 0 when the setting is unset. The |undefined arm is unreachable once settings load, so any later frontend check like config.anonymousDeviceLimit === undefined intended to detect "not configured" silently never fires and always takes the wrong branch; until a consumer lands, this is speculative public surface whose declared type misstates runtime reality.

[ADVISORY] This diff introduces a second, independent copy of the 30-day device-retention window: anonymousDeviceExpiration here in anonstore and an identically-named anonymousDeviceExpiration in pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/api/api.go, both governing the same logical window (count/update enforcement vs the admin ListDevices view). Tuning retention in one package without the other desynchronizes limit enforcement from what the devices API reports, and the shared name gives false confidence that they are one constant; exporting it from anonstore (which anonimpl already imports) deletes the duplication.

[ADVISORY] updateDevice smuggles the SQL string into the variadic args slice (args = append([]interface{}{query}, args...)) instead of calling dbSession.Exec(query, args...), which the session API supports directly and which the rest of the codebase uses. Every maintainer reading this must decode the non-idiomatic query-as-first-argument encoding against xorm's Exec contract before touching the function, and the pattern invites copy-paste into helpers where the prepend runs again, corrupting the statement; the append line is deletable as-is.

[BUG] The device limit is enforced with a non-atomic check-then-act: CreateOrUpdateDevice runs CountDevices and the subsequent upsert as separate statements with no transaction or lock, so concurrent first-time requests all observe count < deviceLimit and all insert. An operator who sets device_limit=N to cap anonymous device tracking gets overshoot under exactly the burst load the feature exists to guard: a flood of unique-cookie requests against a near-empty or near-full table admits more than N devices (multi-replica deployments share the window and widen it), so the PR's headline invariant — at most device_limit devices — is not actually enforced.

[ADVISORY] The diff replaces fire-and-forget device tagging (background goroutine with a 2-minute timeout and panic recovery) with a synchronous TagDevice call inside Authenticate, unconditionally — including the default device_limit=0 deployments that never enable the feature. Every Grafana instance with anonymous access now blocks anonymous authentication on DB round-trips (upsert with the feature off; COUNT+upsert with it on) that previously ran in the background: a slow or hung DB that used to cost only a warn log now stalls anonymous page loads until the client disconnects, and a disconnect mid-request cancels device writes that previously completed; this behavior change is not gated on the new config knob, so it lands on all deployments as drift beyond 'add a configurable device limit'.

[ADVISORY] The new enforcement path is untested: the only added test covers the store rejecting a new device id, while updateDevice's success path (an existing in-window device still admitted and updated when the cap is full) and the end-to-end TagDevice-to-Authenticate rejection branch (client.go:44-50) have no test. A regression in updateDevice's WHERE clause or argument order makes every existing device's update match zero rows and return ErrDeviceLimitReached once the cap fills — locking out all anonymous users — and any error wrap without %w anywhere in tagDeviceUI's path converts enforcement into a warn log so the limit silently stops being enforced; both regressions ship green under the current suite.

[ADVISORY] The PR ships anonymousDeviceLimit to every browser in the boot settings (pkg/api/frontendsettings.go:198) and adds matching TS types, but no code in the diff reads the value, and because the Go field is a non-pointer int64 with no omitempty the payload always carries it — 0 when the feature is off — so the declared `number | undefined` type (packages/grafana-data/src/types/config.ts:200) and the `= undefined` default in GrafanaBootConfig never materialize at runtime. This is public config-surface work not traceable to any requirement in the PR (a dead payload broadcast to all unauthenticated clients, including the anti-abuse cap value itself), and the first future consumer that checks `=== undefined` to distinguish 'unset' from 'disabled' silently misreads every default deployment as explicitly configured.

[ADVISORY] The 30-day device window now exists as two independently maintained same-named constants — anonymousDeviceExpiration in the anonstore package (drives limit enforcement in database.go:108-118 and the updateDevice window) and this copy in the api package (drives the admin device list at api.go ListDevices) — even though this package already imports anonstore. A single-point edit to either constant desynchronizes the admin-facing device list from the limiter's view of what counts against the cap: an operator inspecting cap pressure sees devices the limiter already treats as expired (or misses devices it still counts), with no compile-time or test signal of the drift.

[ADVISORY] When device_limit > 0, CreateOrUpdateDevice issues a COUNT query before every uncached device upsert, and once the cap is full each new-device request pays the COUNT plus an UPDATE that matches zero rows. The abuse-prevention feature adds two DB statements per request precisely during the flood of unique-cookie requests it exists to guard against, multiplying DB load on the anonymous auth path at the worst moment; the COUNT's BETWEEN filter runs on updated_at and the diff adds no migration or index for it.

[ADVISORY] The diff parses the new auth.anonymous device_limit key but adds no corresponding entry to conf/defaults.ini — the file is untouched by the PR — breaking Grafana's convention that every setting appears commented in the shipped template next to its section peers (enabled, org_name, org_role, hide_version). Operators who discover knobs by reading the shipped ini template never learn device_limit exists; the feature ships undiscoverable and undocumented even though its parser sits directly beside the documented auth.anonymous keys.

[ADVISORY] The synchronous replacement for the removed goroutine drops the deliberate deferred recover() that isolated TagDevice panics from the authentication path, even though keeping recover() around the sync call would not interfere with returning the limit error. Any panic in the tagging path — the exact event the old code's 'Tag anon session panic' handler existed to absorb — now propagates out of Authenticate and fails the anonymous request outright instead of being logged and skipped.

[ADVISORY] ErrDeviceLimitReached is a bare fmt.Errorf (anonstore/database.go:19) with no sentinel recognition, HTTP status mapping, or dedicated log/metric key anywhere in the diff, so it propagates out of the authn client as an undifferentiated authentication error. Operators who enable the feature cannot distinguish 'cap reached, working as designed' from 'anonymous auth is broken' in logs and dashboards, and anonymous users hitting the cap get an opaque generic failure with no signal that the instance is at its device limit.

[ADVISORY] updateDevice admits an existing device only if its stored updated_at falls within [device.UpdatedAt−30d, device.UpdatedAt+1min], where device.UpdatedAt is the handling server's clock, making the one-minute forward tolerance the only clock-skew guard in the design. In a multi-replica deployment whose clocks diverge by more than one minute, an existing device last tagged by the ahead-clock replica lands outside the window and is rejected with ErrDeviceLimitReached once the cap is full — a device holding a legitimate slot gets an intermittent auth failure that only manifests when the limit is reached, which no test or comment covers.

[BUG] ProvideAnonymousDeviceService changed its parameter from the injected anonStore anonstore.AnonStore to sqlStore db.DB and now constructs the store itself, while ProvideAnonDBStore (database.go:50-51) gained a required deviceLimit int64 argument, yet the diff updates no production wiring site — Grafana's checked-in DI wire-up in pkg/server still constructs these providers with the old signatures. The tree as diffed does not compile: the generated wiring passes an AnonStore where db.DB is now required and calls ProvideAnonDBStore(store) without the limit argument, and the wire graph cannot even be regenerated because nothing provides a bare int64 — the diff updates only test call sites, not the server construction path.

[BUG] CreateOrUpdateDevice enforces the device limit with a non-transactional COUNT-then-write sequence — CountDevices and the subsequent insert/update run in separate sessions with no lock, serializing transaction, or constraint bounding the table — so K concurrent first-requests from distinct new devices all read count < deviceLimit and all insert. The configured cap is only advisory under exactly the bursty anonymous traffic it exists to cap: concurrent page loads overshoot device_limit by up to concurrency-minus-one devices, and each overshoot row then holds a slot for 30 days (the count window is updated_at within 30 days), leaving the operator's configured limit permanently exceeded.

[ADVISORY] The over-limit rejection path records no state — ErrDeviceLimitReached is returned before any local-cache entry is written and there is no negative caching or backoff anywhere in the new code — so every subsequent request from every blocked device re-runs the full CountDevices range query plus the failing UPDATE. A Grafana page load fires dozens of parallel requests, so blocked anonymous traffic converts its entire request rate into per-request DB load on anon_device (the admitted population costs one refresh per 29 minutes), meaning the very population the limit is meant to exclude now drives the heaviest sustained DB load on the anonymous auth path.

[ADVISORY] The new hot-path CountDevices call filters anon_device solely on an updated_at BETWEEN range, and the diff ships no index or migration supporting that predicate. On deployments whose anon_device table has no updated_at index (none is created in this diff; the only prior time-range consumer was the rare admin ListDevices API), every uncached or rejected anonymous request full-scans a table this same feature deliberately allows to grow to device_limit rows plus 61 days of retained history, collapsing DB CPU once an operator sets a high limit.

[ADVISORY] The device limit is a single global first-come-first-served budget over device identities derived from client-controlled input (IP + User-Agent), with each admitted slot held until 30 days after its last activity and no per-source fairness, org scoping, or automatic reclamation other than the 30-day window. Any population that varies IP or User-Agent — mobile-carrier IPv6 prefix rotation, privacy browsers, trivial scripted rotation — mints a new device per variant and consumes the global budget, so ordinary or low-effort malicious anonymous traffic exhausts the limit and every legitimate anonymous viewer (public dashboards, embeds) is rejected with ErrDeviceLimitReached for up to 30 days, recoverable only via manual admin deletion.

[ADVISORY] The ErrDeviceLimitReached branch returns the raw anonstore sentinel directly into the authn pipeline with no service-side log line, no metric, and no mapping to an authn/HTTP error type — every other tagging failure gets a Warn log while this one is completely silent. Once an operator enables device_limit, mass rejections of anonymous users are invisible in server logs and metrics (indistinguishable from any other auth failure), and clients receive whatever generic status the untyped error path produces instead of a designed limit-reached response, making the feature's main operational state undiagnosable.

[ADVISORY] TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit covers only the reject branch (limit=1, unknown device produces ErrDeviceLimitReached); the at-limit admit branch — an already-admitted device refreshing while count >= limit must match its own row via updateDevice's BETWEEN window and succeed — is exercised by no test in the diff. A regression in the updateDevice window or the rowsAffected handling (e.g., tightening the BETWEEN bounds or mishandling driver-specific affected-row semantics) hard-locks every existing anonymous user out the moment the limit is reached, while the entire test suite stays green.

[ADVISORY] Converting TagDevice from a detached goroutine (own 2-minute timeout context and a recover() guard) to a synchronous call on the request context removes both the hard timeout and the panic isolation, adding an unbounded DB dependency directly inside the anonymous auth path. A slow or saturated database now stalls every cache-miss anonymous request for as long as the request lives (previously capped at 2 minutes and off the request path entirely), and a panic in the tagging path — the reason the recover existed — propagates into the request handler instead of being contained.

[ADVISORY] The new device_limit key is read from the auth.anonymous section but the diff adds no entry to conf/defaults.ini, which documents every neighboring auth.anonymous key (enabled, org_name, org_role, hide_version). Operators cannot discover the feature this PR exists to deliver — the setting is absent from the shipped reference config template and from any config-diff tooling, and the 0-means-unlimited sentinel is undocumented, so the cap ships effectively undiscoverable.

[ADVISORY] The published GrafanaConfig interface gains anonymousDeviceLimit: number | undefined as a required property, but the backend always serializes the field as a number with 0 encoding unlimited (no omitempty, MustInt64(0) default), so the undefined arm is unreachable and the two sides of the contract disagree on the unlimited sentinel. The first frontend consumer written against the declared type distinguishes unlimited via !== undefined and misreads the backend's 0 as a zero-device limit — and nothing in this diff consumes the field at all, so it ships as unread contract surface while out-of-tree implementers of the now-wider required interface stop compiling.

[ADVISORY] ProvideAnonymousDeviceService now constructs the concrete *AnonDBStore internally (anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore(sqlStore, cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit)) instead of receiving the AnonStore interface, hard-wiring the only implementation into the service when injecting *setting.Cfg into the store provider would have preserved the abstraction. The AnonStore interface becomes uninjectable — service-level tests can no longer substitute a fake store (they already reach into the private anonStore field), and adding a decorator or alternate store later requires re-inverting the DI this diff removed.

[ADVISORY] device_limit is parsed with MustInt64(0), so any unparsable value (a typo, 1e6, a thousands-space) silently falls back to 0, which the store interprets as no limit because of the deviceLimit > 0 gate. A malformed cap silently disables enforcement entirely — the fail-open opposite of the neighboring enabled=...MustBool(false), which fails closed — so an operator's licensing or cost limit is unknowingly off with no warning logged.

[BUG] Anonymous.Authenticate escalates anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached into a hard authentication failure (return nil, err), converting the PR's stated objective — a configurable cap on tracked devices, which the store layer itself implements as graceful degradation ('if device limit is reached, only update devices') — into unannounced anonymous access denial. Once device_limit is reached, every request from a new anonymous device fails authentication: 'device limit reached' is a plain fmt.Errorf, not a typed authn error carrying a status, so the authn middleware answers with a 500 internal error instead of the Grafana app — anonymous access silently breaks for new visitors the moment the operator opts in, existing devices keep working, and nothing user-facing explains the 500s.

[BUG] Device tagging moved from the removed background goroutine (detached context.Background() with a 2-minute timeout) onto the synchronous request path via ctx, inverting the accepted constraint that telemetry never blocks anonymous auth — for every deployment, including the default device_limit=0 that never opted in. Every anonymous request with a cold per-process local cache now waits on the DB write before the identity returns, so DB latency and lock contention land directly on anonymous page loads; and a client that disconnects mid-auth cancels ctx, the write fails, and that device is never recorded — undercounting the very telemetry this service exists to collect, where the removed goroutine's detached context guaranteed completion.

[BUG] The deferred recover() from the removed goroutine — whose log message 'Tag anon session panic' shows panics in the tagging path were a known, deliberately contained occurrence — was not replaced anywhere, so a panic during the now-synchronous TagDevice call propagates out of Authenticate into the request. A panic in the tagging path, the exact occurrence the recover() existed to absorb, now escapes Authenticate and kills the request mid-auth (net/http recovers it by closing the connection and dumping a stack trace), flipping a previously invisible telemetry fault into a user-visible request failure.

[BUG] The device limit is enforced by a non-atomic check-then-act: CountDevices runs as one statement and the subsequent insert as another, with no transaction, lock, or constraint tying them together. With count at limit-1, concurrent first requests from different new devices — burst traffic, or normal spread across a multi-node deployment — all observe count < deviceLimit and all insert, so anon_device ends above the configured device_limit; the one invariant the PR exists to guarantee does not hold under the concurrency it was written for.

[BUG] updateDevice's WHERE clause accepts a stored updated_at only up to device.UpdatedAt + time.Minute, so a row last written by a node whose clock runs more than a minute ahead of the serving node fails the BETWEEN predicate and is reported as over-limit. In a multi-node deployment with more than a minute of clock drift — or on a single node after an NTP step-back — an established anonymous device well inside the 30-day window matches zero rows, is returned as ErrDeviceLimitReached, and is denied access even though the limit design explicitly keeps existing devices working.

[ADVISORY] anonymousDeviceLimit is plumbed end-to-end to every browser session (FrontendSettingsDTO → getFrontendSettings → GrafanaConfig in grafana-data and grafana-runtime) but no code in the diff reads it, shipping dead public surface that marks the user-facing half of the feature as dropped mid-review. Operators who set device_limit see anonymous users bounced with raw 500s while the browser receives a number nothing renders; the next developer must guess whether the consuming UI was deliberately cut or lost, and until then the setting is configurable in ini, serialized into every settings payload, and inert.

[ADVISORY] The diff's only test for the limit (TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit) asserts the failure path alone; no test exercises updateDevice's success path for an existing device at the limit, and no test covers Anonymous.Authenticate's mapping of ErrDeviceLimitReached to an auth failure. The two behaviors most likely to regress are unguarded: a change that breaks updateDevice's BETWEEN window locks out all anonymous devices, existing ones included, once the limit is hit, and the single errors.Is check in client.go — the only line between a tracking condition and every anonymous request 500ing — can be deleted with no failing test.

[ADVISORY] The 30-day active-device window now exists twice under the identical identifier anonymousDeviceExpiration — newly added here and the renamed copy in anonimpl/api/api.go (formerly thirtyDays) — with no shared source of truth even though the rename shows the author recognized the coupling. The limit-count window and the admin ListDevices window are equal only by copy-paste; the next editor who changes one constant (say, extending tracking to 60 days) silently desynchronizes device-limit accounting from what the admin device API reports, and neither the compiler (separate packages) nor any test catches the divergence.

[ADVISORY] When a limit is configured, every cache-miss device write now runs a windowed COUNT over anon_device first, and once the limit is reached each rejected new device additionally executes a doomed UPDATE before erroring. At the limit, each denied anonymous request costs two synchronous DB round trips — COUNT plus an UPDATE matching zero rows — on the auth path that the pre-diff code served with one fire-and-forget upsert, so an operator enabling device_limit adds DB pressure at precisely the moment the instance is at capacity.

[ADVISORY] ProvideAnonymousDeviceService's parameter was changed from the anonstore.AnonStore interface to a raw db.DB so the concrete store can be constructed inline (anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore(sqlStore, cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit)), deleting the service's injection seam purely as a wiring convenience for passing the limit. The service can no longer be handed a fake or alternative AnonStore — impl_test.go already pays the price, reaching into the private anonService.anonStore field to list devices, so every future service test is welded to a real DB and a store-level change (caching wrapper, different backend) demands provider surgery instead of a drop-in implementation.

[BUG] CreateOrUpdateDevice enforces the device limit with a check-then-act race: CountDevices runs in its own autocommit DB session and the subsequent upsert runs in another, with no lock, shared transaction, or constraint coupling, so concurrent requests that all observe count < deviceLimit each insert a row and the configured limit is exceeded by the full size of the concurrent burst. An unauthenticated client sends a single parallel burst of N requests carrying distinct device IDs against a configured limit of, say, 10, and all N pass the count check before any insert commits, creating N anon_device rows — the admin-configured cap (and the bound on table growth it exists to impose) is never enforced under exactly the adversarial traffic it targets, and the window is shared across all Grafana instances in HA deployments since they race on the same table.

[ADVISORY] Authenticate now calls TagDevice synchronously on the anonymous request path, replacing the detached goroutine with its 2-minute timeout and recover(), so every anonymous authentication performs blocking DB work (an anon_device upsert, plus a COUNT range-scan when device_limit is set) for any device ID not in the 29-minute local cache — i.e., for every fresh device ID, regardless of whether device_limit is configured. Unauthenticated callers who rotate the client-supplied device ID (the local cache is keyed by that ID) convert each cheap request into blocking DB round trips on the auth critical path: DB slowness or pool saturation now stalls or breaks all anonymous access instead of being isolated in a background goroutine, handing an unauthenticated attacker a direct lever on request-serving capacity; making the call synchronous was needed to surface the limit error, but nothing bounds the blocking DB work the way the deleted timeout did.

[ADVISORY] The device limit is enforced against a global pool of client-supplied device IDs with no per-IP or per-source scoping, and an unauthenticated client can both register device_limit-many arbitrary IDs while under the cap and keep them permanently counted by replaying them, since updateDevice refreshes updated_at for any known ID inside the 30-day window. An attacker spends device_limit cheap unauthenticated requests to saturate the pool, after which every request from any new anonymous device returns ErrDeviceLimitReached and fails authentication — a persistent unauthenticated denial-of-service against the entire anonymous access feature (public dashboards), maintainable indefinitely by occasionally replaying the registered IDs to keep their rows fresh, with no operator tooling in this diff to purge specific attacker devices (only DeleteDevicesOlderThan exists).

[ADVISORY] Replacing the goroutine deletes the defer/recover() whose log message ('Tag anon session panic') documents that this exact TagDevice call has panicked in production, and the new inline call runs on the authentication path with no equivalent containment. Any request input that previously triggered the recovered-and-logged panic (TagDevice parses attacker-controlled headers, remote addresses, and user agents via httpReqCopy) now propagates the panic out of Anonymous.Authenticate into the authn middleware, turning a contained background warning into a 500 on an unauthenticated endpoint, and a panic in the newly added updateDevice path escapes containment the same way.

[ADVISORY] Successful device tags populate the 29-minute local cache but the ErrDeviceLimitReached denial path writes no cache entry anywhere in the new flow, so once the limit is saturated every request from a non-registered device re-executes the full COUNT plus the failing UPDATE synchronously — denials take the expensive verification path on every request while grants are served from cache. The saturated state — which an unauthenticated attacker creates once and maintains for free — is the most DB-expensive state to serve: each hammering request costs two blocking DB round trips with no negative caching, rate limiting, or backoff to shed the load, so the amplification introduced by the synchronous call is maximal exactly in the condition an attacker creates cheapest.

[ADVISORY] The only test added for the device-limit feature, TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit, exercises exclusively the failure branch of updateDevice (rowsAffected == 0 → ErrDeviceLimitReached) by switching the second call to a device_id ("keep") that was never inserted; no test in the diff (scanned: database_test.go's three tests and impl_test.go's two tests) ever drives the success branch — limit reached, device already exists inside the 30-day window, row updated, nil returned. A regression that makes the UPDATE never match a row — swapped BETWEEN window bounds, mis-ordered parameters from the `args = append([]interface{}{query}, args...)` prepend, or a backend RowsAffected quirk — keeps CI green while every returning anonymous device receives ErrDeviceLimitReached, which client.Authenticate converts into a failed authentication, locking out existing anonymous users the moment a device_limit is configured.

[ADVISORY] The only changes to impl_test.go adapt the constructor call; every test builds the service with setting.NewCfg(), whose AnonymousDeviceLimit is the zero value 0, so no test in the diff drives TagDevice through the new limit branch, through the newly added `return err` propagation in TagDevice, or verifies that cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit is wired through ProvideAnonymousDeviceService into anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore. The service-level wiring and TagDevice's changed error contract ship with zero coverage: a mis-wire (wrong cfg field, dropped deviceLimit argument) or an error wrapping that breaks errors.Is(err, anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached) in client.go surfaces only in production, where the limit either silently never applies or anonymous devices start failing authentication.

[BUG] The device limit is enforced as a non-atomic check-then-act — CountDevices runs in one statement and the insert/update in another, with no transaction, row locking, or constraint — so concurrent CreateOrUpdateDevice calls each observe count < deviceLimit and all insert, exceeding the configured cap. An operator who sets auth.anonymous device_limit as a cap gets one that a burst of concurrent new anonymous devices (exactly the traffic the limit polices, and which the per-instance localCache keyed by device id does not serialize across instances) exceeds; the only limit test, TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit, calls CreateOrUpdateDevice strictly serially, so CI cannot detect this.

[ADVISORY] Authenticate now invokes TagDevice synchronously on the request path, deleting the goroutine's recover() guard (the old code explicitly logged "Tag anon session panic") and its 2-minute timeout, so every cache-miss anonymous authentication now blocks inline on the store's COUNT + upsert and a panic or hang in tagging code fails the request instead of being isolated. Every Grafana instance with anonymous auth enabled — including deployments with no device_limit configured, where the write previously ran fire-and-forget — now couples anonymous request latency to database health, and any panic in the tagging path (which the previous code defended against) surfaces as a failed authentication instead of a warning log.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] ErrDeviceLimitReached is a bare fmt.Errorf (anonstore/database.go:19) with no sentinel recognition, HTTP status mapping, or dedicated log/metric key anywhere in the diff, so it propagates out of the authn client as an undifferentiated authentication error. adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] updateDevice admits an existing device only if its stored updated_at falls within [device.UpdatedAt−30d, device.UpdatedAt+1min], where device.UpdatedAt is the handling server's clock, making the one-minute forward tolerance the only clock-skew guard in the design. In a multi-replica deployment whose clocks diverge by more than one minute, an existing device last tagged by the ahead-clock replica lands outside the window and is rejected with ErrDeviceLimitReached once the cap is full — a device holding a legitimate slot gets an intermittent auth failure that only manifests when the limit is reached, which no test or comment covers.

adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: Both comments flag the same underlying problem: the time-window bounds for accepting an existing device are computed using `device.UpdatedAt` (a server-clock-derived timestamp) in a way that can be inconsistent/unsafe across replicas and timezones. The candidate expands on the practical impact (clock skew causing rejections) but it’s the same core issue as the golden note about inconsistent time reference and recommending a consistent `time.Now().UTC()` approach.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] CreateOrUpdateDevice enforces the device limit with a non-transactional COUNT-then-write sequence — CountDevices and the subsequent insert/update run in separate sessions with no lock, serializing transaction, or constraint bounding the table — so K concurrent first-requests from distinct new devices all read count < deviceLimit and all insert. The configured cap is only advisory under exactly the bursty anonymous traffic it exists to cap: concurrent page loads overshoot device_limit by up to concurrency-minus-one devices, and each overshoot row then holds a slot for 30 days (the count window is updated_at within 30 days), leaving the operator's configured limit permanently exceeded.

adjudication.rationale: In `CreateOrUpdateDevice`, the device-limit check is implemented as `CountDevices(...)` followed by a separate insert/update path. The count is performed before building/executing the write, and there is no transaction spanning the count and the subsequent insert/upsert (the only shown transactional wrapper is in `updateDevice` via `WithDbSession`, and it is invoked only after the count says the limit is reached). Under concurrent requests from new devices, multiple goroutines can observe `count < s.deviceLimit` and all proceed to insert/upsert, overshooting the configured limit. The diff shows no locking, serializable transaction, or DB constraint to make the cap strict, so the finding is a real correctness issue in bursty traffic.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The over-limit rejection path records no state — ErrDeviceLimitReached is returned before any local-cache entry is written and there is no negative caching or backoff anywhere in the new code — so every subsequent request from every blocked device re-runs the full CountDevices range query plus the failing UPDATE. A Grafana page load fires dozens of parallel requests, so blocked anonymous traffic converts its entire request rate into per-request DB load on anon_device (the admitted population costs one refresh per 29 minutes), meaning the very population the limit is meant to exclude now drives the heaviest sustained DB load on the anonymous auth path.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a device-limit path in `AnonDBStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice` that, when `count >= s.deviceLimit`, runs `CountDevices(...)` and then attempts `updateDevice(...)`, which returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached` when `rowsAffected == 0` (i.e., device not present/eligible). Nothing in the shown diff adds any negative caching/backoff around this error; `Anonymous.Authenticate` now calls `TagDevice` synchronously and returns the error on `ErrDeviceLimitReached`, so a blocked client can repeatedly trigger the `CountDevices` range query plus the failing `UPDATE`. The specific claim about “before any local-cache entry is written” can’t be fully verified because `tagDeviceUI`/cache-write code isn’t shown, but the per-request DB work on the over-limit path is directly evidenced by the new store logic.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new hot-path CountDevices call filters anon_device solely on an updated_at BETWEEN range, and the diff ships no index or migration supporting that predicate. On deployments whose anon_device table has no updated_at index (none is created in this diff; the only prior time-range consumer was the rare admin ListDevices API), every uncached or rejected anonymous request full-scans a table this same feature deliberately allows to grow to device_limit rows plus 61 days of retained history, collapsing DB CPU once an operator sets a high limit.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new hot-path DB operation in `AnonDBStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice`: when `s.deviceLimit > 0` it calls `s.CountDevices(ctx, now-30d, now+1m)` on each create/update attempt before deciding whether to upsert or fall back to `updateDevice` (which itself predicates on `updated_at BETWEEN ...`). This can materially change performance characteristics for anonymous requests. The diff does not include any schema/migration/index change to support the new time-range predicate, so the concern about potential table scans (if `anon_device.updated_at` isn’t indexed) is a concrete, diff-grounded performance/operational risk rather than a correctness bug. However, the existence/absence of an index in prior migrations is not verifiable from this diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The device limit is a single global first-come-first-served budget over device identities derived from client-controlled input (IP + User-Agent), with each admitted slot held until 30 days after its last activity and no per-source fairness, org scoping, or automatic reclamation other than the 30-day window. Any population that varies IP or User-Agent — mobile-carrier IPv6 prefix rotation, privacy browsers, trivial scripted rotation — mints a new device per variant and consumes the global budget, so ordinary or low-effort malicious anonymous traffic exhausts the limit and every legitimate anonymous viewer (public dashboards, embeds) is rejected with ErrDeviceLimitReached for up to 30 days, recoverable only via manual admin deletion.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does implement a single global cap on “active” anonymous devices: `AnonDBStore` is constructed with a single `deviceLimit` and `CreateOrUpdateDevice` enforces it by `CountDevices(...)` over a 30-day window (`anonymousDeviceExpiration`) and, when full, refuses to insert new devices and instead only attempts an `UPDATE` for the provided `device_id`, returning `ErrDeviceLimitReached` if no row updates. This is not a coding mistake per se, but it does create a real availability/fairness concern grounded in the change: the budget is global (no org/source scoping) and can be exhausted by many distinct device IDs, causing later anonymous viewers to be rejected. However, the finding’s specific claim that identities are derived from IP+User-Agent and that recovery is only via manual deletion is not fully verifiable from this diff (the device ID derivation and any cleanup jobs aren’t shown, and the 30-day window itself provides eventual automatic relief).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The ErrDeviceLimitReached branch returns the raw anonstore sentinel directly into the authn pipeline with no service-side log line, no metric, and no mapping to an authn/HTTP error type — every other tagging failure gets a Warn log while this one is completely silent. Once an operator enables device_limit, mass rejections of anonymous users are invisible in server logs and metrics (indistinguishable from any other auth failure), and clients receive whatever generic status the untyped error path produces instead of a designed limit-reached response, making the feature's main operational state undiagnosable.

adjudication.rationale: In `pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/client.go`, `Authenticate` now calls `TagDevice` synchronously and explicitly returns the raw `anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached` (`if errors.Is(err, anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached) { return nil, err }`) without emitting the `Warn` log used for other tagging failures. The diff also shows no translation of this sentinel into an authn/HTTP-specific error type or any metric/logging path for limit hits, so operators would not see a distinct warning when `device_limit` starts rejecting new devices.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit covers only the reject branch (limit=1, unknown device produces ErrDeviceLimitReached); the at-limit admit branch — an already-admitted device refreshing while count >= limit must match its own row via updateDevice's BETWEEN window and succeed — is exercised by no test in the diff. WHERE device_id = ? AND updated_at BETWEEN ? AND ?` window and `RowsAffected()` semantics. adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] Anonymous.Authenticate escalates anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached into a hard authentication failure (return nil, err), converting the PR's stated objective — a configurable cap on tracked devices, which the store layer itself implements as graceful degradation ('if device limit is reached, only update devices') — into unannounced anonymous access denial. Once device_limit is reached, every request from a new anonymous device fails authentication: 'device limit reached' is a plain fmt.Errorf, not a typed authn error carrying a status, so the authn middleware answers with a 500 internal error instead of the Grafana app — anonymous access silently breaks for new visitors the moment the operator opts in, existing devices keep working, and nothing user-facing explains the 500s.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] Device tagging moved from the removed background goroutine (detached context.Background() with a 2-minute timeout) onto the synchronous request path via ctx, inverting the accepted constraint that telemetry never blocks anonymous auth — for every deployment, including the default device_limit=0 that never opted in. Every anonymous request with a cold per-process local cache now waits on the DB write before the identity returns, so DB latency and lock contention land directly on anonymous page loads; and a client that disconnects mid-auth cancels ctx, the write fails, and that device is never recorded — undercounting the very telemetry this service exists to collect, where the removed goroutine's detached context guaranteed completion.

adjudication.rationale: The diff does verifiably move device tagging from an async goroutine with `context.Background()` + 2m timeout to a synchronous call on the request `ctx` in `pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/client.go` (removed goroutine; now `a.anonDeviceService.TagDevice(ctx, ...)`). This means anonymous auth can now wait on `TagDevice` (which ultimately hits the DB via `CreateOrUpdateDevice`), and cancellation of `ctx` can abort the write. However, the diff doesn’t prove an explicit correctness contract that “telemetry must never block auth,” and respecting request cancellation may be intentional. The issue is therefore a concrete performance/behavior/architecture concern introduced by the change, not a clearly broken or incorrect behavior on its own.

A panic in the tagging path, the exact occurrence the recover() existed to absorb, now escapes Authenticate and kills the request mid-auth (net/http recovers it by closing the connection and dumping a stack trace), flipping a previously invisible telemetry fault into a user-visible request failure.

adjudication.rationale: The diff clearly removes the goroutine wrapper and its deferred `recover()` in `pkg/services/anonymous/anonimpl/client.go` and replaces it with a synchronous `a.anonDeviceService.TagDevice(ctx, ...)` call with no panic protection. adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The device limit is enforced by a non-atomic check-then-act: CountDevices runs as one statement and the subsequent insert as another, with no transaction, lock, or constraint tying them together. With count at limit-1, concurrent first requests from different new devices — burst traffic, or normal spread across a multi-node deployment — all observe count < deviceLimit and all insert, so anon_device ends above the configured device_limit; the one invariant the PR exists to guarantee does not hold under the concurrency it was written for.

adjudication.rationale: In `CreateOrUpdateDevice`, enforcement is implemented as a separate `CountDevices(...)` call followed by a separate insert/upsert path when `count < s.deviceLimit` (and `updateDevice` only when `count >= limit`). The diff shows no transaction, lock, or DB constraint tying the count and subsequent write together, so concurrent requests can all observe `count` below the limit and all insert, exceeding `deviceLimit`. adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] updateDevice's WHERE clause accepts a stored updated_at only up to device.UpdatedAt + time.Minute, so a row last written by a node whose clock runs more than a minute ahead of the serving node fails the BETWEEN predicate and is reported as over-limit. In a multi-node deployment with more than a minute of clock drift — or on a single node after an NTP step-back — an established anonymous device well inside the 30-day window matches zero rows, is returned as ErrDeviceLimitReached, and is denied access even though the limit design explicitly keeps existing devices working.

adjudication.rationale: In `updateDevice`, the `WHERE` clause requires `updated_at BETWEEN device.UpdatedAt-30d AND device.UpdatedAt+1m`. adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The limit check is a non-atomic count-then-act: CountDevices and the subsequent insert run as separate statements with no transaction or lock, so concurrent first-time requests each observe a count below the limit and all proceed to insert. Any concurrent burst of new visitors (or a deliberately parallel bot fleet) overshoots the configured cap by as many requests as race past the count, so an operator who sets device_limit=N sees more than N active devices in the admin device list with no error or log anywhere explaining the overshoot.

adjudication.rationale: In `AnonDBStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice`, the new limit enforcement does `CountDevices(...)` and, only if `count >= s.deviceLimit`, switches to `s.updateDevice`; otherwise it proceeds to insert/upsert (`INSERT ...`/`ON CONFLICT` depending on DB type). This is a classic non-atomic check-then-act: the count query and the subsequent insert/upsert are separate DB operations with no transaction/lock shown in the diff, so concurrent requests can all observe `count < limit` and each insert a new device, overshooting the configured `device_limit` without returning `ErrDeviceLimitReached`.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] ErrDeviceLimitReached is propagated to the authn broker as a bare store sentinel with no mapping to an HTTP status anywhere in the diff, so a deliberate capacity-policy rejection is rendered through whatever generic error path the auth middleware applies to unknown client errors. Users who exceed the device cap receive a generic internal/auth error response instead of a 4xx/429-style policy rejection, so browsers and uptime monitoring read a configured limit as a server malfunction, operators get 5xx alert noise with no attributable signal, and clients cannot distinguish 'retry later' from 'broken'.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows a new sentinel error `anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached` returned from the DB store when the cap is hit (`CreateOrUpdateDevice` -> `updateDevice` returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached` when no rows updated). That error is now propagated up through `AnonDeviceService.TagDevice` (impl.go now `return err` on UI tagging failure) and then out of the authn client (`Anonymous.Authenticate` returns `nil, err` when `errors.Is(err, anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached)`). Within the shown changes there is no translation of this policy rejection into a specific HTTP/authn error type/status; it’s just a bare error value returned from `Authenticate`, so the finding’s concern about an unmapped error path is grounded in the diff. However, the exact HTTP status ultimately produced can’t be verified from this diff alone (it may be handled elsewhere in auth middleware), so it’s not provable as a definite bug here.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The diff turns tagDeviceUI failures into authentication-aborting errors for the device-limit case but leaves the only origin log statement at Debug level, even though every tagging failure was Warn-logged before this change. Operators who enable device_limit get no log evidence at default verbosity when their users start being rejected — the newly user-fatal failure class produces no Warn/Error line on this path — so 'anonymous users suddenly see errors' incidents cannot be diagnosed from logs without raising the log level or reproducing the rejection.

adjudication.rationale: Verified: TagDevice now returns the error from tagDeviceUI (impl.go adds `return err` after a Debug log). Anonymous Authenticate now calls TagDevice synchronously and *suppresses* the Warn log when `errors.Is(err, anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached)` (client.go returns the error immediately). Thus, when device_limit is hit and a new device cannot be updated, the user-facing auth failure can occur with only a Debug-level log (`a.log.Debug("Failed to tag device for UI"...)`) and no Warn/Error on that path, reducing diagnosability at default log levels.
